rungs.stem: In old Irish myth a dark-winged bird was known to settle on shield-rims and spear-points as an army lined up for battle -- and whichever side she chose was the side about to die. The Tuatha De Danann called this bird-shape one of their goddesses in the shape she liked best. Which goddess flies over the battlefield as a crow?
rungs.context: The Morrigan is the war-and-prophecy goddess of the Tuatha De Danann; her most famous shape is the crow (badb) settling on the doomed side of a fight. Brigid is the goddess of poetry, flame, and healing; Danu is the mother-goddess whose name is in Tuatha De Danann itself; Aine is a summer sun-goddess of Munster. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Morrigan.

rungs.stem: The name 'MORRIGAN' is Old Irish and scholars argue about which of two meanings it really carries -- both fit her, but only one puts 'queen' in front of a word for terror or a phantom. Which reading is that darker one?
rungs.context: The two competing readings are 'Great Queen' (from Old Irish mor, great) and 'Phantom Queen' (from a root connoting terror and nightmare); modern scholarship tends to prefer the second. Crow Queen and Silver Queen are not attested readings. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Morrigan.

rungs.stem: In the Book of Invasions the Morrigan is not one goddess but a trio -- three war-sisters, daughters of Ernmas, together known as 'the Morrigan.' One is Badb, the Scald-Crow battle-hag. One is Anand (sometimes called Nemain, 'Frenzy'). The third has her name still stamped on the ancient royal seat of Ulster and on the modern city of Armagh. Who is she?
rungs.context: Macha is the horse-and-sovereignty sister; EMAIN MACHA (Navan Fort, the seat of the Ulster kings) and ARD MACHA ('Macha's Height,' modern Armagh) both bear her name. Brigid, Boann (the goddess of the River Boyne), and Etain are all other great Tuatha De women. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Macha.

rungs.stem: The old Irish new year fell on the night of November 1, when farmers brought their cattle down from summer pasture and the barrier between the mortal world and the Otherworld was said to thin. It is the same night the Morrigan chose for her most famous meeting at the ford before Moytura, and its distant descendant is what English speakers now call Halloween. What is the Irish name of that night?
rungs.context: SAMHAIN (November 1) is the ancestor of modern Halloween -- one of the four quarter-festivals of the Irish year. Bealtaine (May 1) opens summer; Lughnasadh (August 1) is the harvest festival of Lugh; Imbolc (February 1) is the spring festival of Brigid. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samhain.

rungs.stem: On the eve of Samhain, in the days before the Tuatha De's great fight with the Fomorians, the chief-god of the Tuatha De came down to a stream in what is now County Sligo looking for the Morrigan. He found her straddling the water -- one foot on the north bank, one foot on the south, washing herself at the water. Which of the Tuatha De met her there?
rungs.context: The Dagda -- 'the Good God' -- is the chief of the Tuatha De and the Morrigan's partner in the sacred-marriage tryst that seals the Tuatha De's war-alliance with the goddess of the land. Lugh is the war-leader, Nuada the deposed king, Ogma the champion. Source: Cath Maige Tuired section 84; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Dagda.

rungs.stem: The stream where the Dagda met the Morrigan straddling the water was the ford on one particular river, in Corann near modern Riverstown -- and the ford-tryst on Samhain has been fixed there in the sagas ever since. On which river is that ford?
rungs.context: The Unius flows through Corann in County Sligo; the Morrigan's ford is on it, near Riverstown. The Boyne is the river of Newgrange (Aengus's mound); the Shannon is the longest river in Ireland; the Liffey runs through Dublin. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Morrigan; Cath Maige Tuired section 84.

rungs.stem: In return for lying with the Dagda at the ford, the Morrigan pledged she would go alone against the Fomorian king before the battle and cripple him from within. In the words of Cath Maige Tuired she promised to take from him 'the blood of his heart and the kidneys of his valour.' Which Fomorian king did she name?
rungs.context: Indech mac De Domnann is the Fomorian king the Morrigan promises to un-man; the pledge is preserved verbatim in Cath Maige Tuired section 84. Balor is the one-eyed champion killed by Lugh; Bres is the half-Fomorian king the Tuatha De once tried and deposed; Elatha is Bres's father. Source: celt.ucc.ie Cath Maige Tuired section 84.

rungs.stem: In her most terrifying face the Morrigan appears far from any battle -- a woman met alone at a stream in the shallows, rinsing out bloody armor. She never speaks first. If you ask whose armor she has in her hands, she answers with your own name. Which of these is her name in that grim apparition?
rungs.context: The Washer at the Ford is a death-omen: her appearance means the person she names will die that day. Cuchulainn met her on the day of his own death and understood. The Cailleach is the old woman of winter; the Lady of the Lake is Arthurian; the Green Lady is a later British-folklore figure. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Morrigan.

rungs.stem: The wailing woman of later Irish folklore -- the ghostly figure who is heard keening outside a house on the night the head of the family is about to die -- is a folk descendant of the Morrigan's Washer-at-the-Ford face. Her name in Irish means 'woman of the fairy-mound.' What is the wailing woman called?
rungs.context: BEAN-SIDHE ('woman of the sidhe,' anglicised as BANSHEE) is the folk-shadow of the Washer at the Ford -- an aos si woman heard keening for a coming death. The Puca is a shape-changing sidhe trickster; the Leanan-Sidhe is a fairy-lover; the Cailleach is the old woman of winter. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Banshee.

rungs.stem: In the fight itself the Morrigan stood above the battlefield and chanted a rousing rosc that broke the Fomorian nerve, and after the Fomorian king Balor was killed she chanted a second poem -- one that celebrated the victory and then rolled straight on into a dark prophecy of the world's end: 'summer without blossoms, cattle will be without milk, women without modesty, men without valour...' At the end of which battle did she chant that prophecy?
rungs.context: The prophecy is preserved in Cath Maige Tuired sections 166-167 at the close of the SECOND battle of Moytura (Tuatha De vs Fomorians). The First Battle of Moytura was the Tuatha De against the Fir Bolg. The Cattle Raid of Cooley is Cuchulainn's saga. The Battle of Ventry is a Fenian-cycle tale. Source: celt.ucc.ie Cath Maige Tuired sections 166-167.

rungs.stem: The Morrigan's meeting with the Dagda at the ford on Samhain is not merely a love-story but a formal pattern that recurs across Indo-European myth: the god of the tribe unites with the goddess of the land, and the marriage seals the tribe's right to rule and win. Scholars have a name for that pattern. Which name?
rungs.context: The SACRED MARRIAGE (Greek hieros gamos) is the recurring pattern: the tribal god weds the land-goddess to bind land and rule. The Morrigan-and-Dagda ford-tryst is the classic Irish example. The hero's journey is a modern (Campbell) analytic frame; the world tree is a cosmology motif; the twilight of the gods is Ragnarok. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Morrigan; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sacred_marriage.

rungs.stem: The Morrigan's closing rosc at Moytura -- 'I shall not see a world which will be dear to me...' -- rolls straight from a battle-cry into a foretelling that stands beside two other famous Western poems in the same shape: the Norse Voluspa (Odin questioning the seeress) and one Christian book of the New Testament that closes the Bible with a vision of the last days. Which book is that?
rungs.context: REVELATION (the Apocalypse of John) closes the New Testament with the final-days vision -- the Western Christian counterpart to the Morrigan's rosc and to the Voluspa. Daniel and Isaiah contain apocalyptic passages but are Old Testament; Genesis opens the Bible, it does not close it. Source: celt.ucc.ie Cath Maige Tuired sections 166-167; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Book_of_Revelation.
